title: Bag of Tricks for Efficient Text Classification
summary: The paper addresses the problem of achieving competitive text classification accuracy while training and evaluating orders of magnitude faster than deep neural models on large corpora. It proposes fastText, a shallow linear model with a shared low-rank embedding layer, averaged n-gram features, optional hierarchical softmax, and asynchronous SGD on multicore CPUs. It reports that fastText is often on par with deep classifiers, e.g., 92.5% AG News accuracy with h=10 and bigrams, and can train on more than one billion words in less than ten minutes.

match_target.why: User hint explicitly targets Table 1 AG News test accuracy for fastText h=10 with bigrams; it is cheap (seconds per epoch on CPU) and directly demonstrates the paper's central claim that a simple fastText model with bigrams is competitive with deep classifiers.

tolerance.why: Rule 2: no std is reported for the target; it is an accuracy-like % metric on AG News test split, which has 7,600 examples (>2,000), so absolute band = 1.0.

requirements.stmt: Implement the shallow fastText architecture: embed each n-gram feature, average embeddings into a hidden text representation, and feed that representation to a linear classifier/softmax.
requirements.quote: The word representations are then averaged into a text representation, which is in turn fed to a linear classifier.

requirements.stmt: Train by minimizing the negative log-likelihood over classes using the normalized bag of features for each document.
Use asynchronous stochastic gradient descent on multiple CPUs with a linearly decaying learning rate.
requirements.quote: This model is trained asynchronously on multiple CPUs using stochastic gradient descent and a linearly decaying learning rate.

requirements.stmt: Support hierarchical softmax based on a Huffman coding tree for large output spaces, reducing training complexity to O(h log2(k)).
requirements.quote: we use a hierarchical softmax (Goodman, 2001) based on the Huffman coding tree (Mikolov et al., 2013).

requirements.stmt: Use bag-of-n-grams features as additional features to capture partial local word order.
requirements.quote: we use a bag of n-grams as additional features to capture some partial information about the local word order.

requirements.stmt: Map n-grams with the hashing trick using the same hash function as Mikolov et al. (2011), with 10M bins if only bigrams are used and 100M otherwise.
requirements.quote: with the same hashing function as in Mikolov et al. (2011) and 10M bins if we only used bigrams, and 100M otherwise.

requirements.stmt: For the sentiment analysis target, use the same fastText parameters across all datasets, with 10 hidden units and with/without bigrams as reported in Table 1.
requirements.quote: FastText has been run with the same parameters for all the datasets.

requirements.stmt: For the sentiment target, run 5 epochs and select the learning rate on a validation set from {0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5}.
requirements.quote: run fastText for 5 epochs with a learning rate selected on a validation set

requirements.quote: We employ the same 8 datasets and evaluation protocol of Zhang et al. (2015).

requirements.quote: We remove the words and tags occurring less than 100 times and split the data into a train, validation and test set.

requirements.stmt: For tag prediction, run fastText for 5 epochs and compare hidden sizes 50 and 200, with and without bigrams.
requirements.quote: We run fastText for 5 epochs and compare it to Tagspace for two sizes of the hidden layer

data.name: AG News (sentiment analysis)
data.how_to_get: Use the AG News dataset from the 8-dataset sentiment analysis collection of Zhang et al. (2015); the paper links the fastText repository, which can be used for supervised classification examples.

data.name: YFCC100M tag prediction dataset
data.how_to_get: Use YFCC100M from Thomee et al. (2016); the paper says a script to recreate the filtered train/validation/test split will be released, so use that script if available or reconstruct with min-count 100 and the stated split sizes.
